477.title: He wept over it (Luke 19:41–44)
477.hook: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem: if thou hadst known the things for peace
477.howItsDone: Pilgrims in the Holy Land celebrate Mass at the Dominus Flevit chapel on the Mount of Olives, facing the old city, and Catholics pray for peace in Jerusalem and in places at war in the prayers of the faithful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten servants with one pound each, and one who buried his in a napkin. Your line was trade with it. What did you unwrap? Day four hundred seventy-seven, a new week.

On the western slope of the Mount of Olives there's a small church shaped like a teardrop. It was built in the 1950s, and its name is Latin: Dominus Flevit, the Lord wept. Inside, behind the altar, a big window looks straight across the valley at the old city of Jerusalem, so the priest at Mass faces the view. And on the front of the altar is a mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks. The church marks one moment. Jesus has come down the hill on a colt, with crowds shouting praise. And then, at the sight of the city, he stops. Today, he wept over it.
screen: `A CHURCH SHAPED LIKE A TEAR.` → `DOMINUS FLEVIT: THE LORD WEPT.` → `A WINDOW FACING THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Picture the scene. It's what Christians call Palm Sunday. Crowds are spreading their cloaks on the road, shouting blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord. It's the happiest procession in the Gospel. And in the middle of it, Luke says: "And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it." Luke's word here means to weep aloud, to sob, not just to have tears in your eyes. Then he speaks to the city: "If thou also hadst known, and that in this thy day, the things that are to thy peace; but now they are hidden from thy eyes." The things that are to thy peace. There's a play on words in it. Many people heard the name Jerusalem as containing shalom, peace. The city of peace, he says, hasn't recognized what makes for peace. Then he grieves over what's coming: enemies will surround the city, and not leave a stone upon a stone, because thou hast not known the time of thy visitation. Christians later read these words in light of what happened about forty years after: in the year 70 the Roman army besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple, and many thousands died. It's important to hear this the way Jesus says it. He doesn't gloat. He doesn't curse. He weeps, the way you'd weep over a child running toward a road. Remember the hen, a few chapters back: how often would I have gathered thy children. It's the same love. Catholics hear in this a God who isn't distant from the suffering of cities. Before the stones fall, someone stood on a hill and cried for them by name.
screen: `THE HAPPIEST PROCESSION, THEN TEARS.` · `WEPT ALOUD, NOT A QUIET TEAR.` · `THE CITY OF PEACE MISSED PEACE.` · `GRIEF, NOT GLOATING.` · then, large: `THE THINGS THAT ARE TO THY PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a city at war. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one city in the world where people are living through war or violence right now. If a name comes, use it. Picture it from a hill, the way Jesus saw Jerusalem: rooftops, streets, a market, a hospital, children going somewhere. Let yourself feel something for the people there, without needing to fix it or take a side. If you pray, ask for the things that make for peace there. If you don't, hold them in your attention with care. The bell holds the time.
He wept over it. Jesus, at the sight of Jerusalem in the middle of a joyful procession, sobbing over a city that didn't know the things for its peace. Today's word.
Your line: the things for peace. Today, when you hear news of a city in conflict, stop for one breath and wish it peace. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

Luke places it during the entry, as the crowds shouted praise.

it means to weep aloud, to sob.
Jesus cursed Jerusalem when he saw it
he wept over it and grieved for what was coming.

fork.setup: you're riding into a city to cheers and palm branches. you look up and see it spread out below you. what happens?
options: you wave to the crowds.
you weep over the city.
you speed up to reach the Temple.
fork.reveal: Luke says he wept over it: if thou hadst known the things that are to thy peace.

original.note: Greek: he wept aloud, sobbed. A stronger word than the quiet tears at Lazarus' tomb in John.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was sad that people rejected him.
what it means: he grieves for the city itself and for what will happen to its people, because it didn't know what made for peace.
what a scholar hears: Luke uses eklausen, loud weeping; John 11:35 uses edakrusen, shed tears. Many heard shalom in the name Jerusalem.

478.title: Not one stone (Luke 21:1–6)
478.hook: the widow's mites, then the Temple's beauty and its end
478.tomorrow: Do this for a commemoration of me
478.howItsDone: Catholics bring offerings to the altar at the offertory of every Mass, and parishes sometimes point to the widow's mite when they speak of giving: not the size of the gift, but how much of yourself is in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the middle of the palms. Your line was the things for peace. Which city did you hold? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

Two scenes sit side by side in Luke, within six verses, both in the Temple. In the first, Jesus watches rich people casting their gifts into the treasury, a steady clink of coins. Then a poor widow drops in two brass mites. In the second, some people are admiring the building itself: its goodly stones, and the gifts that adorn it. A tiny gift, and a vast one. Today, which one lasts.
screen: `THE CLINK OF RICH PEOPLE'S COINS.` → `TWO BRASS MITES.` → `GOODLY STONES AND GIFTS.`

segments.voice: First the widow. The Douay calls her coins two brass mites; Luke's Greek calls them lepta, small coins. Jesus says: "Verily I say to you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all." The others gave out of their abundance. She gave out of her want, all the living that she had. Jesus doesn't measure the amount. He measures what was left after. Then, a moment later, people are praising the Temple. They had reason. This was the Temple Herod the Great had rebuilt, and Josephus, who saw it, says that from a distance it looked like a snowy mountain, white stone and gold. And Jesus says: "The days will come in which there shall not be left a stone upon a stone that shall not be thrown down." Yesterday he said it weeping, on the hill. Today he says it standing among the stones themselves. Put the two scenes together and they ask one question: what lasts? The great stones, admired by the crowd, did not. The two coins, noticed by Jesus, are still read aloud wherever this Gospel is read. Luke isn't saying buildings are bad. Catholics build cathedrals. He's asking where a heart rests. Stones, however beautiful, fall. A gift of the whole self is remembered.
screen: `TWO BRASS MITES IN THE TREASURY.` · `MORE THAN THEY ALL.` · `A TEMPLE LIKE A SNOWY MOUNTAIN.` · `STONES FALL. THE GIFT REMAINS.` · then, large: `NOT A STONE UPON A STONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treasure what won't fall. Settle, and breathe. Make a quiet list in your head of what you're proud of, or worried about keeping: a house, a title, a body, a reputation, a bank balance. Hold each one a moment, and let it be what it is: good, and temporary. Then bring to mind something that lasts: a love you've given, a kindness someone still remembers, faith, if you have it. Rest there. If you pray, offer God something small and whole, like the widow's two coins. The bell holds the time.
Not one stone. Jesus' word about the beautiful Temple, spoken just after a poor widow's two coins: the stones will fall, the whole-hearted gift lasts. Today's word.
Your line: what lasts. Today, give one small thing with your whole heart, and let it be enough that God notices. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

screen: `DAY 478 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.`

what it means: Jesus measures a gift by what's left afterward; she gave everything, and that outlasts the Temple's stones.
what a scholar hears: Josephus describes Herod's Temple as like a snow-covered mountain; it was destroyed by Rome in the year 70.

479.title: Do this for a commemoration of me (Luke 22:14–20)
479.word: Do this for a commemoration of m
479.hook: Luke's words of institution, the root of the Mass
479.howItsDone: At every Mass the priest repeats the words of institution over the bread and wine, and Catholics kneel or bow at the elevation; on Holy Thursday the Church celebrates the Mass of the Lord's Supper, remembering this night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow's two coins and the Temple's great stones. Your line was what lasts. What did you give with your whole heart? Day four hundred seventy-nine.

The words a priest says over the bread at every Mass were first spoken, Luke says, in an upper room in Jerusalem. Luke even tells how the room was found. Jesus sends Peter and John ahead to prepare the Passover, and tells them to follow a man carrying a pitcher of water into a house. The owner shows them a large upper room, furnished, just as Jesus said. The hour comes, and he sits down at table with the twelve apostles. Today, the words at the root of the Mass.
screen: `THE WORDS SAID AT EVERY MASS.` → `A LARGE UPPER ROOM, FURNISHED.` → `THE HOUR COMES.`

segments.voice: Luke begins with longing. Jesus says: "With desire I have desired to eat this pasch with you, before I suffer." The doubled phrase is a way of saying: I have wanted this so much. Then a detail Luke records: two cups. Early in the meal Jesus takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them to share it, saying he won't drink again of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom comes. Some readers connect this with the cups of wine at the Passover meal. Then the bread: "And taking bread, he gave thanks, and brake; and gave to them, saying: This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." And after supper, the second cup: "This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you." Now, today's word. Commemoration, in the Greek, is anamnesis. It doesn't mean a nostalgic memory, like looking at an old photo. The Passover command already speaks this way: Exodus tells each parent to explain the feast as what the Lord did for me, when I came out of Egypt. Remembering, there, makes the saving event present. Catholics believe that at Mass the one sacrifice of Christ is made present, not repeated, and that the bread and wine become his body and blood, which the Church calls transubstantiation. The Council of Trent also taught that with the words do this, Christ made the apostles priests. Other Christians understand these words in different ways: many Protestants see the supper as a memorial and a meal of faith. All of them start from this same table and this same command. Notice its size. Not believe this, or understand this, first. Do this.
screen: `WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED.` · `TWO CUPS IN LUKE.` · `THIS IS MY BODY, GIVEN FOR YOU.` · `ANAMNESIS: MEMORY MADE PRESENT.` · then, large: `DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the Last Supper at table. Settle, and breathe. Think about your next meal today. Picture the table, the plate, who'll be there, or that you'll be alone. Now picture, gently, that upper room: thirteen people, bread, a cup, a man who knew what was coming and still gave thanks. When you sit down to eat today, pause for one breath before the first bite. If you pray, give thanks the way he did. If you don't, simply remember that night and the people at it. The bell holds the time.
Do this for a commemoration of me. Jesus' command over the bread in Luke, the words of institution at the root of every Mass. Today's word.
screen: `DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: do this. Today, at one meal, pause before eating and remember the upper room. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

fork.setup: it's your last meal with your friends before you suffer. you take bread in your hands. what do you do first?
options: explain what's about to happen to you.
give thanks.
ask them to remember you.
fork.reveal: he gives thanks first, breaks the bread, and says this is my body, which is given for you. do this for a commemoration of me.

original.note: Greek: remembrance, commemoration. In Catholic theology, the memorial that makes Christ's sacrifice present.

trapdoor: what you thought: do this means remember Jesus fondly over a meal.
what it means: Catholics believe this command makes Christ's one sacrifice present at every Mass, with the bread and wine becoming his body and blood.
what a scholar hears: anamnesis echoes Passover memorial (zikkaron, Exodus 12:14); Trent (Session 22, canon 2) taught do this ordained the apostles priests.

480.title: As one that serveth (Luke 22:24–27)
480.hook: at the supper they argue about greatness; he says I am among you as one that serves
480.howItsDone: Every Catholic priest and bishop is first ordained a deacon, and the Holy Thursday Mass of the Lord's Supper provides for the priest to wash the feet of members of the congregation, in memory of Christ serving at the Last Supper.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bread and the cup in the upper room. Your line was do this. Did you pause before a meal? Day four hundred eighty.

In Luke, the very next thing after the bread and the cup is an argument. Jesus has just said this is my body, given for you. He's just told them one of them will betray him. And the apostles, at that same table, fall to arguing about which of them is the greater. A family bickering over who gets the good chair at a hospital bedside. Mark and Matthew tell of a similar quarrel earlier, on the road; Luke sets it here, at the Last Supper. Today, how Jesus answers it.
screen: `RIGHT AFTER THE BREAD AND CUP.` → `WHICH OF US IS THE GREATER?` → `LUKE SETS IT AT THE SUPPER.`

segments.voice: Luke says: "And there was also a strife amongst them, which of them should seem to be the greater." Jesus doesn't scold them for wanting to matter. He redraws what mattering means. The kings of the nations lord it over people, he says, and the people in power like to be called benefactors. "But you not so." Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves. Then he asks a simple question about the room they're sitting in. Who's greater, the one reclining at table or the one serving? At any dinner the answer is plain: the one at table. "But I am in the midst of you, as he that serveth." He doesn't say I'm like a servant. He says, I am in the midst of you as one serving. Present tense. Right now, at this table. The Greek word is diakonon, the one who waits on tables, from the same family as the word deacon. The Catholic Church builds this into its own shape. Every priest and bishop is first ordained a deacon, a servant, and that service is meant never to wear off. Pope Gregory the Great called himself servant of the servants of God, servus servorum Dei, and popes still use the title at the head of official letters. The pope's own title borrows the job at the bottom of the table. A title doesn't guarantee anyone lives up to it. It names the standard Jesus set at the table, the night before he died: greatness measured by service.
screen: `A STRIFE ABOUT GREATNESS.` · `BUT YOU NOT SO.` · `DIAKONON: THE ONE WHO WAITS TABLES.` · `SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD.` · then, large: `I AM IN THE MIDST OF YOU AS HE THAT SERVETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve without being asked. Settle, and breathe. Picture the rooms you'll be in today: home, work, a bus, a store. Where is there a small job nobody wants? Dishes in the sink, a full trash bag, a spill, a coworker drowning in a task, a parent who's tired. Choose one, and decide to just do it without announcing it or waiting to be thanked. Picture yourself doing it quietly. If you pray, offer it as service. The bell holds the time.
As one that serveth. Jesus' answer to his apostles' argument at the Last Supper: I am among you as the one who waits on the table. Today's word.
Your line: as one that serveth. Today, do one small job nobody asked you to do, and don't mention it. Day four hundred eighty.

options: settle it by naming the greatest.

end the dinner early.

original.note: Greek: the one serving, waiting on tables. The root of the word deacon.

trapdoor: what you thought: as one that serveth is a nice humble saying.
what it means: at his last meal, Jesus places himself in the lowest job at the table and makes that the measure of greatness.
what a scholar hears: diakonon, the one waiting tables; Gregory the Great's title servus servorum Dei is still used by popes.

481.title: Drops of blood (Luke 22:39–46)
481.hook: only Luke tells of the angel and the sweat like drops of blood
481.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Agony in the Garden as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, and some keep a holy hour of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, especially on Holy Thursday night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the apostles argued about greatness, and Jesus said he was among them as one who serves. Your line was as one that serveth. What job did you do unasked? Day four hundred eighty-one.

It's late. The supper is over. Jesus goes out, with his disciples following, to the Mount of Olives, to a place Luke says he went as he was accustomed. A familiar spot. Somewhere he'd prayed before. A chair by a window, a corner of a church, a walk taken when something is too heavy: some people keep a place like that. He tells the disciples to pray that they don't enter into temptation. Then he goes on a little further, about a stone's throw, and kneels down. Today, what happened when he did.
screen: `OUT OF THE CITY, AFTER SUPPER.` → `A PLACE HE WENT AS ACCUSTOMED.` → `A STONE'S THROW FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Kneeling, he prays: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." The chalice is the cup of suffering ahead. He asks honestly for it to pass, and then hands the decision over. And then Luke gives us two details no other Gospel has: "And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony, he prayed the longer. And his sweat became as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground." Look at the order. The angel comes, and the agony doesn't stop. It deepens. He prays the longer. The angel doesn't take the cup away. The angel helps him drink it. In Luke's picture, strength from heaven isn't an exit. It's company in it. Agony, in Luke's Greek, is agonia, a word that could describe an athlete's strain before a contest, as well as deep anguish. And the sweat is like drops of blood: Luke says as, like. Readers have long debated whether he means real blood or a comparison for heavy, dark drops. The text doesn't settle it. Something else worth knowing: some early manuscripts of Luke don't have these two verses. The Church receives them as Scripture, and they're in the Latin Vulgate and the Douay. And the disciples? He comes back and finds them sleeping for sorrow. Luke is gentle with them: it was grief that knocked them out. Catholics pray this moment as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, the Agony in the Garden, and some keep a holy hour, an hour of prayer, remembering that in Matthew and Mark, Jesus asks his friends to watch one hour with him.
screen: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE.` · `AN ANGEL, AND THE AGONY DEEPENS.` · `AGONIA: THE STRAIN BEFORE THE RACE.` · `SLEEPING FOR SORROW.` · then, large: `HIS SWEAT AS DROPS OF BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone in agony. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone going through something terrible right now: a frightening diagnosis, a court date, an addiction, a night in an emergency room, a grief with no bottom. Picture them at their own stone's throw, alone. You can't take the cup away. But you can keep watch. Stay with them in your mind for these two minutes, the way the disciples were asked to. If you pray, ask that they be strengthened, as he was. The bell holds the time.
Drops of blood. Luke's picture of Jesus' agony on the Mount of Olives, his sweat like drops of blood, an angel strengthening him to go on. Today's word.
Your line: an angel strengthened him. Today, be a small strengthening for one person in a hard hour: a message, a visit, a minute of real attention. Day four hundred eighty-one.

Luke 22:43–44 has no parallel in the other Gospels.
Luke blames the disciples harshly for sleeping
he says they were sleeping for sorrow.

fork.setup: you're kneeling alone, a stone's throw from your friends, and the suffering ahead is terrible. what do you pray?

if you will, remove it; but not my will, but yours.
nothing; you just wait.

original.note: Greek: agony, the strain and struggle of a contest; Luke's word for Jesus in the garden.

trapdoor: what you thought: agony just means terrible pain.
what it means: in Luke, it's the struggle of someone straining toward a contest he's chosen to face, and he prays the longer through it.
what a scholar hears: Luke 22:43–44 is missing from some early manuscripts but is in the Vulgate; agonia appears only here in the New Testament.

482.title: The servant's ear (Luke 22:47–53)
482.hook: even while arrested he heals the ear Peter cut off
482.howItsDone: Catholics hear the arrest in the garden in the Passion read on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and the healing of the servant's ear is preached by many as Christ's refusal of violence even in his own defense.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garden: the sweat like drops of blood, and an angel strengthened him. Who did you carry in prayer, or in thought, through their own hard night? Day four hundred eighty-two.

The prayer in the garden is over. Torches come up the hill. A crowd with swords and clubs, and at the front a familiar face: Judas, one of the twelve, leaning in to kiss his teacher. In the dark it all happens fast. Someone near Jesus asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? and doesn't wait for the answer. A blade swings. The servant of the high priest is holding the side of his head, and his right ear is gone. This is the moment a fight starts. Everyone can feel it. Today we watch what Jesus does with that moment, and it is the last healing Luke records before the cross.
screen: `TORCHES IN THE GARDEN.` → `A KISS, THEN A SWORD.` → `A RIGHT EAR CUT OFF.`

segments.voice: All four Gospels tell of the sword in the garden. Only John gives the names: the one with the sword is Simon Peter, and the servant is called Malchus. Only Luke, the doctor's Gospel by old tradition, tells us what happened next. In the Douay-Rheims it reads: "But Jesus answering, said: Suffer ye thus far. And when he had touched his ear, he healed him." Suffer ye thus far. It's an old phrase, and nobody is fully sure of the exact sense of the Greek. Many modern readers hear it as no more of this, or enough, stop here. Others hear Jesus speaking to the crowd: let me go this far, let me reach him. Either way, the fighting ends with a hand on a stranger's wound. Look at who gets healed. Not a friend. Not a disciple. A man who came out at night to arrest him. And look at when. Jesus is about to be bound, and his own hands are the ones still free to touch. Then he turns to the chief priests and captains and says it plainly: they could have taken him any day in the temple, "but this is your hour, and the power of darkness." He names the darkness. He doesn't fight it with a sword. Read slowly, the scene shows how Jesus meets violence: he refuses it, and he repairs what his own side broke. Peter swung the blade. Jesus cleans up after Peter. On an ordinary day that's the part that stings. Most of the damage we have to mend wasn't done by our enemies. It was done by us, or by people on our side, trying to help.
screen: `PETER'S SWORD, MALCHUS'S EAR.` · `SUFFER YE THUS FAR.` · `HE HEALS THE MAN WHO CAME FOR HIM.` · `THIS IS YOUR HOUR.` · then, large: `HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: heal one thing you damaged. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come to mind that broke because of you. A sharp word in a group chat. A borrowed thing returned worse. A friendship you let go quiet on purpose. Don't make a list; just let one come. Picture what touching it would look like. A message. An apology with no excuse attached. Fixing the thing. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to do it. If not, just hold it in front of you and decide one small next step. The bell holds the time.
The servant's ear. Cut off by Peter in the garden, touched and healed by Jesus while the soldiers closed in. Luke alone tells the healing. Today's word.
Your line: no more of this. Today, when an argument starts to swing, say it to yourself, put the sword down, and fix one thing your side broke. Day four hundred eighty-two.

Luke says only "one of them". John's Gospel gives the names Peter and Malchus.

trapdoor: what you thought: a disciple loses his temper and someone gets hurt.
what it means: Jesus ends the violence on his own side and heals the man who came to arrest him.
what a scholar hears: only Luke records the healing; only John names Peter and Malchus. the Greek of "suffer ye thus far" is brief and read more than one way.

483.title: Herod's mockery (Luke 23:6–12)
483.hook: Herod wants a show, gets silence, and he and Pilate become friends
483.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's account of Jesus before Herod in the Passion read on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke, and his silence is sometimes linked in preaching with the suffering servant of Isaiah 53.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the servant's ear: a sword in the garden, and a hand that healed the man who came to arrest him. Your line was no more of this. Did you mend one thing your side broke? Day four hundred eighty-three.

Early morning in Jerusalem. Pilate, the Roman governor, has a prisoner he doesn't want. Then someone mentions that the man is from Galilee. Galilee belongs to Herod Antipas, and Luke says Herod is in Jerusalem in those days. Pilate sees a way out: send him over. So Jesus is walked across town to a different palace, to a different ruler, the son of the Herod from the Christmas story. And this Herod is delighted. He has heard about this man for a long time. He has wanted to meet him. Not to listen. To be entertained. Today, a king who wants a show.
screen: `PILATE PASSES THE PROBLEM.` → `HEROD IS DELIGHTED.` → `HE WANTS A SHOW.`

segments.voice: Only Luke tells this scene, and he tells us what Herod was after. Herod was glad to see Jesus, he says, because he hoped to see some sign done by him. A miracle, on demand, for the court. So Herod questions him, at length. And then the line that gives this day its carry, in the Douay-Rheims: "But he answered him nothing." Not a word. Remember who Herod is. This is the ruler who had John the Baptist beheaded. Earlier in Luke, Jesus calls him that fox. Now the fox has him in the room, and Jesus won't perform. The chief priests stand nearby shouting accusations. Herod and his soldiers, unable to get a reaction, turn to mockery. They treat him with contempt, and the Douay says they sent him back "putting on him a white garment." A costume. A joke about a king. Then Luke adds a strange, quiet sentence: Herod and Pilate became friends that same day, though before they had been enemies. Two rulers who couldn't stand each other found common ground in a prisoner they both refused to take seriously. Some readers hear in this silence Isaiah's suffering servant, who opened not his mouth. It isn't sulking, and it isn't weakness. It's a refusal to turn the holiest things into a party trick for someone who only wants to watch. There are moments every day when someone wants a performance from us: the clever comeback, the outrage, the show for the audience. Silence before Herod is a way of saying, I won't play that part.
screen: `HEROD HOPED TO SEE A SIGN.` · `BUT HE ANSWERED HIM NOTHING.` · `A WHITE GARMENT, A JOKE OF A KING.` · `ENEMIES BECOME FRIENDS THAT DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't perform for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you put on a show. A meeting where you try to sound clever. A feed where you post for applause. A relative who always gets the version of you they expect. Picture yourself there, quieter. Not cold, not sulking. Just declining the act. Notice what changes when there's nothing to prove. If you pray, you can bring that place to God and ask to be the same person in it. The bell holds the time.
Herod's mockery. A ruler who wanted a miracle for entertainment, got silence, and dressed Jesus up as a joke. Today's word.

Your line: silence before herod. Today, skip one performance. And that's week sixty-nine: he wept over the city, not one stone, do this, as one that serveth, drops of blood, the servant's ear, and Herod. Day four hundred eighty-three.
